content: Favus, derived from the Latin word for honeycomb, is a fungal disease primarily affecting the scalp but can also occur on other areas of the skin and, in rare cases, on mucous membranes. The disease is characterized by the presence of yellowish, circular, cup-shaped crusts known as scutula. These crusts are grouped in patches resembling a honeycomb and are approximately the size of a split pea, with a hair projecting from the center of each lesion. Over time, the lesions enlarge and become crusted, with the characteristic honeycomb-like appearance visible only at the edges of the scab. As the disease progresses over several months, the scabs and scutula eventually detach, leaving behind shiny, hairless patches of skin. Favus is a chronic condition that can persist for 10 to 20 years if untreated. It is caused by the growth of a fungus, and the pathological changes observed are the tissue's reaction to the fungal invasion. The disease was first identified as fungal in origin by Johann Lukas Schönlein in 1839, marking the first discovery of a fungal disease. Schönlein's findings were published in a brief note in Miller's Archive that year. The fungus was later named Achorion schoenleinii by Robert Remak in honor of Schönlein. The name Achorion referred to a microscopic structure observed in infected skin scrapings, consisting of slender, matted mycelial threads bearing oval, nucleated fungal spores (arthroconidia), either free or joined. This structure is now referred to as scutula. The fungus itself is currently classified as Trichophyton schoenleinii. During the initial stages of infection, fungal spores are believed to penetrate the unbroken skin surface and germinate primarily in and around the hair follicles, sometimes extending into the hair shaft. In 1892, Paul Gerson Unna described two additional forms of the fungus: Favus griseus, which produces grayish-yellow scutula, and Favus sulphureus celerior, which causes sulfur-yellow scutula with rapid growth. These classifications were made before the rigorous distinction between microorganism identities and disease identities became standard in scientific practice. As a result, these older, ambiguous disease-based names are no longer recognized in modern mycology or dermatology. Historically, favus was widespread globally, and before Schönlein's recognition of its fungal etiology, it was often misdiagnosed as Hansen's disease (leprosy). This misdiagnosis led to European patients being confined to leprosaria. However, with the advent of modern antifungal therapies, particularly the introduction of griseofulvin, favus has been eradicated in most parts of the world. Today, it is primarily found in rural areas of Central Asia and scattered rural regions of Africa. The disease is closely associated with poverty and geographic isolation but is highly treatable, making it one of the diseases most likely to be completely eliminated through modern medicine. Occasionally, infections resembling favus may be caused by other dermatophyte fungi, often diagnosed as atypical inflammatory tinea. These infections may rarely be attributed to common soil-borne dermatophytes such as Microsporum gypseum or Trichophyton mentagrophytes. The latter, in its post-1999 classification, refers to a phylogenetic species formerly known as Trichophyton mentagrophytes var. quinckeanum, which is also the causative agent of favus infections in mice.
